summary: Children learn to draw and identify polygons by their defining attribute — a pentagon is ANY closed figure with five straight sides whose sides do not cross each other, not one memorised 'textbook' shape. The core obstacle is the prototype effect: learners draw and accept only the regular, symmetrical, horizontal-base version and miss irregular, tilted or rotated members of a class. Guidance centres on generating many varied and irregular examples, defining each class by its attribute (side/vertex count, closed, straight-sided, sides not crossing), and hunting for ALL members in mixed sets that include non-prototypical and near-miss shapes. Accurate side/vertex counting is scaffolded by marking each once.
misconceptions: Draws or accepts only the prototypical regular, symmetrical, horizontal-base example and misses irregular or rotated members of a class.
Miscounts sides or vertices when drawing or identifying (draws six sides when asked for five; loses track counting an irregular shape).
Draws a non-closed figure or one with curved sides, not attending to 'closed' and 'straight-sided'.
Judges class membership by the name/look ('that's not a quadrilateral, it's a diamond') rather than by counting the sides.

activities.title: Build a polygon to a target side-count
steps: Given an instruction such as 'build a shape with exactly five straight sides', construct the figure on dotted paper, a geoboard, or a peg/rubber-band grid.
Count and mark each side (and vertex) once as it is drawn, so the total is checked rather than guessed.
Ensure the figure CLOSES and that every side is straight before declaring it finished.
When one valid shape is made, draw 'a different pentagon that does NOT look like the first one' — a long, spiky, or irregular one.
Compare a regular and an irregular example of the same class side by side and state why both satisfy the attribute.
activities.insight: A polygon class is defined by its attribute (number of straight sides meeting at vertices, closed figure with sides that do not cross), invariant to size, orientation and regularity — not by matching a single remembered prototype.

activities.title: Find them all in a mixed set
steps: From a mixed set that includes regular, irregular, tilted, rotated and near-miss shapes plus non-examples, mark EVERY member of a named class (e.g. 'circle all the quadrilaterals').
For each shape marked or skipped, justify by counting sides/vertices and checking closed + straight-sided, not by its name or look.
Deliberately inspect the awkward shapes — a long thin tilted four-sided shape, a dented pentagon — and decide membership by the attribute.
Explain why a square is a quadrilateral, and why a 'diamond' is also a quadrilateral regardless of its orientation.
activities.insight: Identifying a class means applying its attribute to every candidate, including irregular and rotated ones, rather than recognising a familiar picture.

activities.title: Name, draw and justify by attribute
steps: Draw a named polygon (e.g. a hexagon) and explain how you know it is one by counting its six straight sides and six vertices/angles.
Produce a second example of the same name that looks clearly different from the first.
State the defining attributes in your own words ('a hexagon is any closed shape with six straight sides that do not cross each other').
activities.insight: Justifying class membership by the attribute count — and producing a non-prototypical second example — demonstrates the definition is understood, not just a remembered shape.

checkQuestion: Set three short tasks and watch how the child works: (1) 'Draw me a shape with exactly five straight sides.' (2) Hand them a mixed set of shapes (including irregular and tilted ones): 'Circle all the quadrilaterals.' (3) 'Draw a hexagon, and show me how you know it is a hexagon.'
checkAnswer: (1) Draws any closed figure with exactly five straight sides — need not be a regular pentagon. (2) Circles every four-sided shape, including irregular and rotated ones, and no others. (3) Draws a six-sided closed figure and justifies by counting six sides (and six vertices/angles). The attribute is satisfied by the count, not by matching a prototype.
